facts.statehood_note: One of the original 13; Maryland became the seventh state when it ratified the U.S. Constitution on April 28, 1788.
facts.nickname: The Old Line State (also called the Free State; neither nickname was ever made official)
facts.motto: Fatti maschii, parole femine (usually translated 'Strong deeds, gentle words'); a traditional motto never formally adopted
facts.name_origin: Named in honor of Henrietta Maria of France, the wife of England's King Charles I, who granted the colony's charter in 1632.

government.chambers: Maryland Senate (47 members) and Maryland House of Delegates (141 members); members of both serve four-year terms.
government.executive: Governor (4-year term), elected with a lieutenant governor. A governor who has served two terms in a row may not run again right away.
government.courts: Supreme Court of Maryland (seven justices, one from each of seven appellate judicial circuits). The governor appoints justices with the Senate's consent; voters then decide whether to keep each justice for a ten-year term. The court was called the Court of Appeals until December 14, 2022.
government.local: 23 counties plus Baltimore City, which together make the state's 24 main local governments; some counties are run by county commissioners, and others have charter or 'home rule' governments.
government.constitution: Current constitution written at a convention in Annapolis (May 8 to August 17, 1867) and ratified by the people on September 18, 1867. The constitution before it, of 1864, ended slavery in Maryland.
government.kid_line: "That all Government of right originates from the People" (Maryland Declaration of Rights, Article 1).

long_ago.about: The Piscataway were one of the largest Chesapeake nations when Europeans arrived. Smaller groups such as the Chaptico later joined Piscataway bands, and Piscataway people still live in southern and central Maryland.
The Nanticoke lived on the Eastern Shore; in 1608 John Smith recorded their main village, Kuskarawaok. Most Nanticoke left Maryland in the mid-1700s, and those who stayed bought land.

The Susquehannock, a nation related to the Iroquois, had villages in today's Cecil, Harford, and Allegany counties. They fought Maryland colonists from 1642 to 1652, then signed a treaty that gave up much of their land near the mouth of the Susquehanna River.
In 1608 John Smith met the Pocomoke on the Pocomoke River. Their lands covered today's Somerset, Wicomico, and Worcester counties on the lower Eastern Shore.
The Choptank, an Algonquin people of today's Dorchester and Wicomico counties, hunted and fished near the Chesapeake Bay in the warmer months.

today.about: Recognized by the State of Maryland on January 9, 2012, among the first tribes Maryland ever recognized.
Also recognized by the State of Maryland on January 9, 2012.
Recognized by the State of Maryland on December 19, 2017; the Accohannock still have a presence in Somerset County.

first_peoples.today_note: Maryland has no federally recognized tribes. The state recognizes the Piscataway (2012) and the Accohannock (2017). The Maryland Commission on Indian Affairs also serves the Assateague Peoples Tribe, the Nause-Waiwash Band of Indians, the Pocomoke Indian Nation, and the Youghiogheny River Band of Shawnee Indians. In the 2020 Census, about 128,650 Marylanders identified as Native American or part Native American.
sites: Havre de Grace Maritime Museum, which displays a replica Susquehannock wigwam
St. Clement's Island and Historic St. Mary's City, where English colonists landed in 1634 and bought land from the Yaocomaco people
Moyaone in Piscataway Park (Accokeek, Prince George's County), a historic Piscataway home on the Potomac River where Piscataway leader Turkey Tayac is buried

history.event: Many Indigenous bands, nations, and confederacies live in the land now called Maryland.
English captain John Smith explores the Chesapeake Bay and records nations including the Pocomoke, Tockwogh, and Nanticoke.
King Charles I of England gives the Maryland charter to Cecilius Calvert, Lord Baltimore, and the colony is named for Queen Henrietta Maria.

On March 25, settlers from the ships Ark and Dove land at St. Clement's Island. They buy land from the Yaocomaco and build St. Mary's City, Maryland's first capital. Mathias de Sousa and Francisco arrive on the same ships.
The Susquehannock fight Maryland colonists. A 1652 treaty takes much of their land and ends most Susquehannock presence in Maryland.
On January 21, 1648, landowner Margaret Brent asks the Assembly for a vote and is refused. In 1649 'An Act concerning Religion' gives religious freedom to Christians who believe in the Trinity.
A Maryland law allows slavery. Over time, planters bring more and more enslaved Africans to the colony.

As colonists take more land, many Algonquin nations, including the Choptank, Nanticoke, Pocomoke, and Assateague, move away, some joining nations in Delaware and Pennsylvania; some families stay and buy land.
Annapolis serves as the nation's capital, and Congress ratifies the Treaty of Paris, which ends the American Revolution, in the Maryland State House.
Maryland becomes the seventh state to ratify the U.S. Constitution.
British forces burn Washington and bomb Fort McHenry in Baltimore. Francis Scott Key writes the 'Star-Spangled Banner.'

Frederick Douglass escapes slavery by train in 1838. Harriet Tubman frees herself in 1849 and returns about 13 times, guiding more than 70 people to freedom, while free Black helpers like Jacob Jackson and Samuel Green aid freedom seekers.
The first bloodshed of the Civil War happens in Baltimore in 1861. On September 17, 1862, the Battle of Antietam near Sharpsburg leaves more than 23,000 casualties.
A new state constitution ends slavery in Maryland on November 1, 1864, with soldiers in the field allowed to vote on it. In 1867 Marylanders ratify a new constitution, still in use today.

trailblazers.name: Turkey Tayac (Philip Sheridan Proctor)
trailblazers.text: Born in Charles County, Maryland, he served in World War I and then spent decades reviving Piscataway culture and pushing for the Piscataway to be recognized as a Native nation. He supported creating Piscataway Park around Moyaone, the historic Piscataway home on the Potomac River, and after his death Congress allowed him to be buried there.

trailblazers.name: Margaret Brent
trailblazers.text: Margaret Brent arrived in Maryland in 1638 and owned land near St. Mary's City. After Governor Leonard Calvert died in 1647, she ran his estate and found ways to pay the colony's unpaid soldiers so they would not rebel. On January 21, 1648, she asked the Assembly for a vote as a landowner and as Lord Baltimore's attorney, and she was refused.

trailblazers.name: Benjamin Banneker
trailblazers.text: Benjamin Banneker was born in Baltimore County and built a working clock made entirely of wood. In 1791 he did the astronomy and math to help survey the boundary of the new national capital, and he published a yearly almanac with tide tables and eclipses, called the first scientific book by a Black American.

trailblazers.name: Josiah Henson
trailblazers.text: Josiah Henson was born into slavery in Charles County in 1789 and was enslaved on Isaac Riley's farm in today's North Bethesda. In 1825 he was sent to Kentucky, and in 1830 he escaped to freedom in Canada. His 1849 life story was a basis for Harriet Beecher Stowe's novel Uncle Tom's Cabin, and the Josiah Henson Museum and Park stands where he was enslaved.

trailblazers.name: Henry Highland Garnet
trailblazers.text: Henry Highland Garnet was born enslaved in 1815 in New Market (now Chesterville), Kent County, Maryland, and escaped with his family in 1824 when he was a young boy. He became a famous abolitionist and minister, and on February 12, 1865, he became the first African American to speak in the chamber of the U.S. House of Representatives, giving a sermon there.

trailblazers.name: Frederick Douglass
trailblazers.text: Frederick Douglass was born into slavery in Talbot County in February 1818. In 1838 he disguised himself as a sailor and escaped by train through Havre de Grace, then became a leading abolitionist, writer, and speaker until his death in 1895.

trailblazers.name: Harriet Tubman
trailblazers.text: Born Araminta Ross in Dorchester County, Harriet Tubman freed herself from slavery in 1849. She returned about 13 times and guided more than 70 people to freedom, then served the Union in the Civil War as a nurse and spy and led a raid on the Combahee River in South Carolina.

landforms: Backbone Mountain, whose Hoye Crest (3,360 feet) in Garrett County is Maryland's highest point
Calvert Cliffs, which line about 24 miles of Chesapeake Bay shore
The Eastern Shore on the Delmarva Peninsula
The Blue Ridge, Ridge and Valley, and Appalachian Plateaus mountains of western Maryland
waters: Chesapeake Bay (about 200 miles long, average depth about 21 feet)
Susquehanna River (which meets the bay at Havre de Grace)
geography.regions: Maryland has six natural regions (physiographic provinces): the Atlantic Continental Shelf, the Coastal Plain in the east around the Chesapeake Bay, the Piedmont Plateau in the center, and the Blue Ridge, Ridge and Valley, and Appalachian Plateaus in the mountainous west.

ecosystems.name: Chesapeake Bay estuary
ecosystems.about: An estuary where river water mixes with salt water; about half the bay's water comes from the Atlantic Ocean. It supports 348 kinds of fish and 173 kinds of shellfish, including the blue crab, Maryland's state crustacean.

ecosystems.name: Tidal marshes and wetlands
ecosystems.about: Marshes like those at Blackwater National Wildlife Refuge in Dorchester County, where Harriet Tubman learned the waterways, are winter homes for birds; about one million ducks, geese, and swans arrive in the bay's watershed each fall.

ecosystems.name: An ancient sea at Calvert Cliffs
ecosystems.about: Between about 10 and 20 million years ago a warm, shallow sea covered southern Maryland. Its sharks, whales, rays, and shellfish are now fossils in the cliffs, with over 600 species found.

science.weather: The east has a humid subtropical climate, and the mountainous west has colder, snowier winters. Snowfall ranges from about 9 inches on the coast to over 100 inches in the western mountains. Maryland averages 30 to 40 thunderstorm days and about six tornadoes a year, can be hit by tropical storms and hurricanes, and has small earthquakes, sinkholes, and landslides.
science.resources: The Chesapeake Bay supports a large seafood industry, and almost 30 percent of the bay's watershed is farmland. Maryland's economy also includes government work, health care, biotechnology, information technology, defense, and universities.
science.highlight: Fossil hunting at Calvert Cliffs State Park: sharks lived in the sea over southern Maryland about 17 million years ago, and visitors sift the beach sand for their teeth, including rare teeth of the giant shark megalodon.

g3_ss.title: Maryland's Communities and Government
g3_ss.plan: Locate Annapolis, Baltimore, the 23 counties and Baltimore City, and learn what the General Assembly's 47 senators and 141 delegates do.

g3_ss.title: Maryland's First Peoples
g3_ss.plan: Meet the Piscataway, Nanticoke, Pocomoke, and Susquehannock, see a Susquehannock wigwam, and learn that Maryland recognized the Piscataway in 2012 and the Accohannock in 2017.

g3_ss.title: Maryland Trailblazers
g3_ss.plan: Make picture biographies of Margaret Brent, Benjamin Banneker, Frederick Douglass, Harriet Tubman, and Piscataway leader Turkey Tayac.

g45_ss.title: Maryland's First Nations
g45_ss.plan: Use John Smith's 1608 records and the Maryland Manual to map where Chesapeake nations lived, then trace how land loss pushed many to move north.

g45_ss.title: Colonial Maryland
g45_ss.plan: Study the 1634 landing on Yaocomaco land, the 1649 religion law, Margaret Brent's request to vote, and the 1664 law that allowed slavery.

g45_ss.title: Maryland 1788–1877
g45_ss.plan: Follow statehood, Fort McHenry, the Underground Railroad (Tubman, Douglass, Henson, Garnet), Antietam, and the 1864 constitution that ended slavery in Maryland.

g3_sci.title: The Blue Crab
g3_sci.plan: Learn the blue crab's body parts and life in the Chesapeake Bay, and why it is the state crustacean.

g3_sci.title: Birds of the Bay
g3_sci.plan: Watch for the Baltimore oriole and learn why about one million ducks, geese, and swans spend winter around the bay.

g3_sci.title: Fossil Detectives
g3_sci.plan: Sort pictures of shark teeth and shells from Calvert Cliffs and talk about what they tell us about an ancient sea.

g45_sci.title: The Chesapeake Bay Estuary
g45_sci.plan: Model how fresh river water and salt ocean water mix, map the 64,000-square-mile watershed across six states, and study bay food webs.

g45_sci.title: Maryland's Six Regions
g45_sci.plan: Compare the Coastal Plain, Piedmont, and western mountains using rocks, elevation, and snowfall from 9 inches to over 100 inches.

g45_sci.title: Reading the Rocks at Calvert Cliffs
g45_sci.plan: Investigate how a sea covered southern Maryland 10 to 20 million years ago, why cliff erosion exposes fossils, and why it is unsafe to climb the cliffs.
